title: Report on Clinical Study Abroad at Warwick University
paragraphs: In Japan, where one third of deaths are due to cancer, I aspire to become a medical oncologist, and I am very interested in what kind of care to provide to cancer patients and how to support them to the very end. The United Kingdom is the birthplace of the hospice, and the history of medical oncology there is long, more than half a century. Also, under the unified system of the NHS, everyone can receive medical care free of charge. This spring I was given the opportunity to do a seven-week clinical clerkship at Warwick University Hospital in the UK, and I went to the UK with two goals: "to understand the mechanism of the NHS, which provides medical care free of charge," and "to understand what kind of care is provided to cancer patients, from diagnosis to treatment and final palliative care."

I spent five weeks in medical oncology and palliative care and two weeks in hematology. In the UK, chemotherapy and radiotherapy in cancer treatment are handled by medical oncologists. For that reason, even when treating cancer patients, surgeons, physicians and medical oncologists always cooperate in the treatment, and treatment policy is decided by a multidisciplinary meeting that further includes radiologists, pathologists, specialist nurses and others. It was impressive that at the meetings, opinions were actively exchanged from the standpoint of each specialist about the optimal care for each patient.

Dr. Franks, who looked after me during the first five weeks, was a somewhat special doctor, a medical oncologist who also holds a qualification in palliative care. In the medical interviews of Dr. Franks, who sees patients who cannot be cured every day, words that could always find hope even within harsh reality were woven in, and there was a gentleness that wrapped around deep sorrow. Each time I was moved to the point of getting goosebumps, and at the same time I felt the difference in the medical environment in that the numbers of both doctors and staff were sufficient enough for him to spend a long time (sometimes about an hour) on each patient's consultation.

Also, when I told him at the start that I was interested in everything from the treatment of cancer patients to end-of-life care, Dr. Franks gave me opportunities throughout the five weeks to meet people of various professions and see their work. Specifically, these were doctors working in adult and children's hospices, a respiratory physician, a chaplain working in the medical setting, a complementary therapist working on the cancer ward, a Macmillan nurse specialising in supporting cancer patients, a lung cancer specialist nurse, an end-of-life care specialist nurse, a dressing specialist nurse, a radiographer, a pharmacist specialising in palliative care, a thoracic surgeon and others. I was surprised at the large number of highly specialised co-medical staff and the closeness of the cross-cutting links among doctors, and at the same time I was once again impressed that roles are properly divided, a system is in place to support cancer patients to the end, including their mental state, and all of that is provided free of charge. Cooperation with community care is also close, and when sending a terminally ill patient home, the end-of-life care specialist nurse, the family and the patient discuss, and local doctors, nurses and others are arranged according to needs. Furthermore, medical equipment, nursing beds, helpers and even a service of keeping someone in attendance 24 hours a day in preparation for a sudden change were provided free of charge, and home care was supported.

In hematology, I accompanied the doctors to learn the whole flow of outpatient and ward work, and within it I was given opportunities to take physical findings and do medical interviews, present them to the doctor in charge and have a question and answer session. I also took part in study sessions for junior doctors, in which I made diagnoses from blood films, and attended classes for the students here. When I accompanied them to a seminar held in the suburbs, I was able to talk in the car with doctors with whom I cannot usually talk at leisure about various things, from the differences between Japanese and British medical care to differences in culture and religion. Also, Dr. Jackson, who looked after me most, invited me to a home party on the last weekend, and afterwards listening to Handel's Messiah in full at the church that he usually attends became a very good memory.

The stimulating and fulfilling seven weeks passed in no time, but I learned a great many hints for thinking about the future of Japanese medical care, especially cancer treatment and end-of-life care. Finally, I would like to express my gratitude to all concerned, beginning with the doctors of the International Exchange Office and everyone in charge of study abroad, who gave me this wonderful opportunity and always supported me. Thank you very much.
